name: Quantitative Methods
blurb: The maths toolkit behind every other topic, rebuilt for 2027 around applications: returns and benchmarks, time value, statistics and distributions, hypothesis testing, portfolio risk and optimization, simulation, CAPM regression and data science. At 11–14% it is now pass-critical.
accaNote: FM gives you TVM, NPV/IRR, the dividend model and CAPM, and MA/PM gives basic statistics and expected values, so the first LMs will feel familiar. Hypothesis testing, regression inference, Bayes, distributions, simulation, portfolio optimization and data science are new.

modules.title: Returns of Financial Assets and Instruments
modules.summary: What an interest rate or required return represents, how it is built up from a real risk-free rate plus inflation and risk premia, and how nominal and real returns relate.

acca.note: FM covered the Fisher relationship (real vs nominal) and the CAPM risk premium. New for CFA: the explicit build-up of an interest rate from inflation, default, liquidity and maturity premiums, and the three interpretations of an interest rate.

lessons.title: Interest rates: three meanings and the build-up

cards.title: One number, three meanings
cards.body:
An interest rate can be read three ways:

- **Required rate of return**: the minimum return an investor needs to accept an investment.
- **Discount rate**: the rate used to bring future cash flows back to today.
- **Opportunity cost**: the return you give up by spending today instead of investing.

Same 6%, three lenses. Exam questions often describe one lens and ask you to name it.

cards.title: Build-up of a nominal interest rate
cards.formula: r = real r_{f} + inflation premium + default premium + liquidity premium + maturity premium
where: return on a riskless, liquid, single-period asset with no inflation
compensation for expected inflation over the life of the instrument
compensation for the chance the borrower does not pay
compensation for difficulty selling quickly at fair value
compensation for greater price sensitivity of longer-dated debt to rate changes
cards.note: Real r_{f} + inflation premium ≈ nominal risk-free rate (e.g. a short-term T-bill yield).

cards.title: Pricing a corporate bond's required rate
cards.body:
Real risk-free 2.0%, inflation premium 3.0%, default 1.5%, liquidity 0.5%, maturity 1.0%.

- 3-month T-bill (no default, liquid, short): 2.0 + 3.0 = **5.0%**
- 10-year corporate bond: 2.0 + 3.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 + 1.0 = **8.0%**

The 3.0% gap is the sum of the three risk premiums.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM taught the Fisher equation and CAPM, but not this premium-by-premium build-up. CFA likes to ask which premium explains a yield difference: same issuer, longer maturity → maturity premium; same maturity, thinly traded bond → liquidity premium; same maturity, lower-rated issuer → default premium.

lessons.title: Nominal vs real returns and risk premia

cards.title: Nominal, real and inflation
cards.note: Approximation: nominal ≈ real + π. Use the exact form when options are close.

cards.title: Exact vs approximate
cards.body:
Real risk-free 1.5%, expected inflation 2.5%.

Exact nominal = 1.015 × 1.025 − 1 = **4.04%**. Approximation gives 4.00%.

Going the other way: nominal 6%, inflation 4% → real = 1.06/1.04 − 1 = **1.92%** (not 2.00%).

cards.title: Risk-free rates and risk premia
cards.body:
The **risk-free rate** is usually proxied by a short-term government bill yield in the asset's currency. Any risky asset's required return = risk-free rate + a **risk premium** for the risks borne.

- Bonds: premium = credit spread (default + liquidity).
- Equities: premium = equity risk premium (ERP), historically larger because equity holders are paid last.

Required return on equity = r_{f} + ERP (single-factor intuition behind CAPM).

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: When the question gives a *nominal* return and asks for a *real* return, divide; do not subtract, unless it says 'approximately'. Also check whether the premiums are stated per year: the build-up uses annual rates.

questions.stem: An investor says she will only buy a bond if it offers at least 7% per year, because she could earn that on a comparable investment. The 7% is best described as her:
questions.explanation: 7% is the minimum return she demands before investing: a required rate of return (it can also be read as an opportunity cost). A maturity premium is only one component of a rate, and the real risk-free rate excludes inflation and all risk premiums.

questions.stem: Two bonds from the same AA-rated issuer are equally liquid. The 10-year bond yields 1.2% more than the 2-year bond. This difference is most likely explained by a:
questions.explanation: Same issuer means the same default risk, and equal liquidity removes the liquidity premium. What remains is the extra price sensitivity of longer-dated debt to rate changes, the maturity premium.

questions.stem: Real risk-free rate 2.0%, inflation premium 3.0%, default premium 1.5%, liquidity premium 0.5%, maturity premium 1.0%. Using the additive build-up, the required rate on a long-term corporate bond is closest to:
questions.explanation: Add all five components: 2.0 + 3.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 + 1.0 = 8.0%. 5.0% is only the nominal risk-free rate (real r_{f} + inflation). 6.5% leaves out the liquidity and maturity premiums.

questions.stem: A government bond offers a nominal return of 6% and expected inflation is 4%. The exact real return is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1.06/1.04) − 1 = 1.92%. 2.00% is the subtraction approximation, and 10.24% compounds the two rates (1.06 × 1.04 − 1) instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Which statement about a risky asset's required return is most accurate? It equals the:
options: nominal risk-free rate plus a risk premium
real risk-free rate plus expected inflation only
nominal risk-free rate minus a risk premium
questions.explanation: Investors demand compensation for bearing risk, so the required return is the nominal risk-free rate plus a risk premium. Real risk-free plus inflation is just the nominal risk-free rate, and subtracting a premium would make risky assets require less than riskless ones.

questions.stem: The nominal risk-free rate is 4% and the equity risk premium is 5.5%. Using the risk-free-plus-premium framework, the required return on an average-risk equity is:
questions.explanation: Required return = r_{f} + ERP = 4% + 5.5% = 9.5%. 5.5% ignores the risk-free rate and 1.5% subtracts the two components.

questions.stem: A thinly traded bond and a heavily traded bond have the same issuer, maturity and coupon. The thinly traded bond's higher yield reflects a:
questions.explanation: Only tradability differs, so the extra yield compensates for the cost and difficulty of selling quickly: a liquidity premium. Maturity and expected inflation are identical for the two bonds.

questions.stem: The real risk-free rate is 1.8% and expected inflation is 2.7%. The exact nominal risk-free rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: 1.018 × 1.027 − 1 = 4.549% ≈ 4.55%. 4.50% is the additive approximation, and 0.88% wrongly treats the real rate as the result of dividing by inflation.

questions.stem: A 3-month T-bill yields 4.0%. A 10-year government bond yields 5.2% and a 10-year BBB corporate bond yields 7.0%, both equally liquid. The default premium on the corporate bond is closest to:
questions.explanation: Compare bonds with the same maturity: 7.0% − 5.2% = 1.8% default premium. 3.0% (7.0 − 4.0) also includes the maturity premium; 1.2% (5.2 − 4.0) is the maturity premium.

questions.stem: An analyst uses 8% to convert a payment due in 3 years into today's value. In this use, 8% is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Converting a future amount into a present value is discounting, so the rate is a discount rate. The real risk-free rate and a liquidity premium are building blocks of a rate, not the role it plays here.

questions.stem: Expected inflation rises by 1% while the real risk-free rate and all risk premiums are unchanged. The required nominal return on a 5-year corporate bond will most likely:
options: stay the same, because real returns are unchanged
questions.explanation: The inflation premium is a component of every nominal rate, so the required nominal yield rises by roughly the increase in expected inflation. The real return stays the same, but the nominal return must rise to keep it there.

flashcards.front: Build-up of a nominal interest rate
flashcards.back: Real risk-free rate + inflation premium + default premium + liquidity premium + maturity premium.

flashcards.front: Three interpretations of an interest rate
flashcards.back: Required rate of return; discount rate; opportunity cost.
(1 + nominal) = (1 + real)(1 + π). Approximation: nominal ≈ real + π.
Real risk-free rate + inflation premium (proxy: short-term government bill yield).
Extra yield for longer-dated debt because its price is more sensitive to interest-rate changes.

flashcards.front: Required return on a risky asset
flashcards.back: Risk-free rate + risk premium (credit spread for bonds, equity risk premium for stocks).

modules.title: Types of Financial Returns
modules.summary: How to calculate and compare holding-period, arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, annualized and continuously compounded returns, and gross/net, after-tax, real and leveraged returns.

acca.note: FM gives you compounding, effective annual rates and real vs nominal. New for CFA: geometric vs arithmetic vs harmonic means, continuously compounded (log) returns and their additivity, and the leveraged-return formula.

lessons.title: Holding-period returns and the three means

cards.title: Holding-period return (HPR)
cards.note: Multi-period: (1 + R_{1})(1 + R_{2})…(1 + R_{n}) − 1. Link returns by multiplying, never by adding.

cards.title: Arithmetic vs geometric mean
cards.note: Geometric ≤ arithmetic; the gap widens as volatility rises. Geometric = the constant rate that reproduces the actual ending wealth.

cards.title: Why the geometric mean matters
cards.body:
Returns: +50%, then −50%.

Arithmetic mean = 0%. But $100 → $150 → $75: you lost money.

Geometric mean = (1.5 × 0.5)^{1/2} − 1 = **−13.40%**, which matches the actual result.

Use arithmetic for a single-period *expected* return; geometric for past compound performance.

cards.title: Harmonic mean
cards.note: Average cost per share when investing the **same amount of money** each period (cost averaging). Harmonic ≤ geometric ≤ arithmetic.

cards.title: Cost averaging
cards.body:
Invest $1,000 at $20, then $1,000 at $25.

Shares = 50 + 40 = 90; average cost = 2,000/90 = **$22.22**.

Harmonic mean = 2/(1/20 + 1/25) = $22.22. The arithmetic mean of prices ($22.50) overstates your cost.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Trimmed mean drops a % of extreme values; winsorized mean replaces them with the nearest remaining value. Both reduce the influence of outliers.

cards.title: Annualizing a return
where: number of periods in a year (12 for monthly, 4 for quarterly, 365/days for a days-based return)
cards.note: Works for periods longer than a year too: an 18-month return uses c = 12/18.

cards.title: Three conversions
cards.body:
- Quarterly 2.5% → 1.025^{4} − 1 = **10.38%**
- Weekly 0.2% → 1.002^{52} − 1 = **10.95%**
- 18-month 9% → 1.09^{12/18} − 1 = **5.91%**

Annualizing a short-period return assumes it can be repeated, which is a strong assumption for volatile assets.

cards.title: Continuously compounded (log) return
cards.note: Log returns are additive over time: r_{cc, 0→T} = Σ r_{cc, t}. This is why simulations and the lognormal model use them.

cards.title: Adding log returns
cards.body:
Price 40 → 46: HPR 15%, r_{cc} = ln(1.15) = **13.98%**.

Three years of log returns: 10%, −4%, 3%. Total r_{cc} = 9%, so HPR = e^{0.09} − 1 = **9.42%**.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Log returns are always lower than the matching HPR when positive (13.98% vs 15%). A rise from 100 to 125 (+22.31% log) and a fall back to 100 (−22.31% log) sum to zero. Simple returns (+25%, −20%) do not.

lessons.title: Gross, net, after-tax, real and leveraged returns

cards.title: Return types
rows: Before management fees (trading costs already deducted)
Return on the investor's own equity when part of the position is borrowed

cards.title: Leveraged return
cards.note: Leverage magnifies returns in both directions: it helps only when R_{p} > r_{D}.

cards.title: Leverage at work
cards.body:
$1,000,000 portfolio: $700,000 equity, $300,000 borrowed at 4%. Portfolio return 7%.

R_{L} = 7% + (300/700)(7% − 4%) = **8.29%**.

If the portfolio earned only 2%, R_{L} = 2% + 0.4286 × (−2%) = 1.14%, worse than unlevered.

cards.title: Stacking adjustments
cards.body:
Gross return 10%, fees 1.5%, tax 20%, inflation 3%.

- Net: 10 − 1.5 = 8.5%
- After tax: 8.5 × 0.8 = **6.8%**
- Real (from the 8.5% net): 1.085/1.03 − 1 = **5.34%**

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: In FM you used effective rates and Fisher. CFA adds the leveraged-return formula and wants you to say which return is relevant to whom: a fund's *gross* return measures the manager's skill; *net* and *after-tax real* returns are what the client actually keeps.

questions.stem: A stock bought at $25.00 pays a $0.75 dividend and is sold at $23.00. The holding-period return is closest to:
questions.explanation: HPR = (23 − 25 + 0.75)/25 = −1.25/25 = −5.00%. −8.00% ignores the dividend. −5.43% divides by the ending price (23) instead of the starting price.

questions.stem: A fund returned +15%, −10% and +5% in three consecutive years. Its geometric mean annual return is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1.15 × 0.90 × 1.05)^{1/3} − 1 = 1.08675^{1/3} − 1 = 2.81%. 3.33% is the arithmetic mean, and 8.67% is the cumulative 3-year return, not an annual average.

questions.stem: An investor puts the same dollar amount into a stock in each of three months at prices of $10.00, $12.50 and $8.00. The average cost per share is closest to:
questions.explanation: Equal amounts of money invested → harmonic mean: 3/(1/10 + 1/12.5 + 1/8) = 3/0.305 = $9.84. $10.17 is the arithmetic mean of prices and $10.00 is their geometric mean; both overstate the cost because more shares are bought when the price is low.

questions.stem: Which measure best describes the compound annual growth rate an investor actually earned over several past years?
questions.explanation: The geometric mean is the constant rate that turns the starting value into the ending value. The arithmetic mean overstates compound growth when returns vary, and the harmonic mean is for averaging prices under cost averaging.

questions.stem: A portfolio earns 1.2% per month. The annualized return is closest to:
questions.explanation: 1.012^{12} − 1 = 15.39%. 14.40% (1.2 × 12) ignores compounding; 14.31% (12 × ln 1.012) is the continuously compounded annual rate, not the effective annual return.

questions.stem: An investment gained 30% in total over three years. Its annualized return is closest to:
questions.explanation: 1.30^{1/3} − 1 = 9.14%. 10.00% simply divides 30% by 3 and ignores compounding. 8.75% is ln(1.30)/3, the continuously compounded annual rate, not the effective annualized return.

questions.stem: A stock's continuously compounded returns over three years are +10%, −4% and +3%. The 3-year holding-period return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Log returns add: 10 − 4 + 3 = 9%. Convert to HPR: e^{0.09} − 1 = 9.42%. 9.00% is the log return itself, not the HPR. 8.77% wrongly treats the log returns as simple returns and compounds them (1.10 × 0.96 × 1.03 − 1).

questions.stem: A $1,000,000 portfolio is financed with $700,000 of equity and $300,000 borrowed at 4%. The portfolio earns 7%. The return on equity is closest to:
questions.explanation: R_{L} = 7% + (300/700)(7% − 4%) = 7% + 1.29% = 8.29%. 7.00% ignores leverage. 10.00% (7/0.7) ignores the interest cost of the borrowed money.

questions.stem: A fund's gross return is 10%, fees are 1.5% and the investor's tax rate is 20%. Her after-tax net return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Net = 10 − 1.5 = 8.5%; after tax = 8.5 × (1 − 0.2) = 6.80%. 8.00% applies tax to the gross return and ignores fees. 6.50% deducts fees after tax (10 × 0.8 − 1.5).

questions.stem: A bond fund returned 8.5% nominal while inflation was 3%. Its real return is closest to:
questions.explanation: 1.085/1.03 − 1 = 5.34%. 5.50% is the subtraction approximation and 11.76% multiplies instead of divides.

questions.stem: A 90-day investment returns 4%. Assuming 365 days in a year and that the return can be repeated, the annualized return is closest to:
An investor finances half of a portfolio with debt costing 8%. The portfolio earns 6%. Her leveraged return is closest to:
questions.explanation: V_{B}/V_{E} = 1, so R_{L} = 6% + 1 × (6% − 8%) = 4.0%. 6.0% ignores leverage. −2.0% is just the spread R_{p} − r_{D}. Because the portfolio earned less than the borrowing cost, leverage reduced the return.

questions.stem: Which statement about arithmetic and geometric mean returns is most accurate?
options: The geometric mean exceeds the arithmetic mean when returns are volatile
The two are equal only when all periodic returns are identical
The arithmetic mean is the better measure of past compound growth
questions.explanation: The geometric mean is always ≤ the arithmetic mean, with equality only when there is no variability in returns. Volatility widens the gap (so a volatile series has a geometric mean *below* its arithmetic mean, not above), and the geometric mean, not the arithmetic, measures compound growth.

questions.stem: A bond bought at 100 pays a 6 coupon and is sold one year later at 92. The holding-period return is:
questions.explanation: HPR = (92 − 100 + 6)/100 = −2.0%. −8.0% ignores the coupon and +6.0% ignores the price fall.

questions.stem: A stock's continuously compounded annual return is 12%. The equivalent effective annual (holding-period) return is closest to:
questions.explanation: HPR = e^{0.12} − 1 = 12.75%. 12.00% confuses the two measures, and 11.33% = ln(1.12) converts in the wrong direction.

flashcards.back: [Π(1 + R_{t})]^{1/T} − 1. Always ≤ arithmetic mean; measures past compound growth.

flashcards.front: Harmonic mean and when to use it
flashcards.back: n/Σ(1/X_{i}). Average cost per share when equal money amounts are invested (cost averaging). Harmonic ≤ geometric ≤ arithmetic.
(1 + R_{period})^{c} − 1, where c = periods per year (e.g. 365/days).
r_{cc} = ln(1 + HPR) = ln(P_{1}/P_{0}); HPR = e^{r_{cc}} − 1. Additive over time.
R_{L} = R_{p} + (V_{B}/V_{E})(R_{p} − r_{D}). Helps only if R_{p} > r_{D}.
Gross = before management fees and admin expenses; net = after them. Gross measures manager skill.

modules.title: Benchmarking Returns
modules.summary: Measuring a portfolio's performance with money-weighted and time-weighted returns, and building the security market indexes used as benchmarks: weighting methods, index values and price vs total returns.

acca.note: FM's IRR is exactly the money-weighted return. New for CFA: time-weighted returns, why managers are judged on TWR, and index construction and weighting (price, market-cap, float-adjusted, equal, fundamental).

cards.title: Two questions, two returns
cards.body:
**Money-weighted return (MWR)** = the IRR of all the investor's cash flows. It answers: *how did the investor's money do?* It is affected by the timing and size of deposits and withdrawals.

**Time-weighted return (TWR)** = the compound growth of $1 invested for the whole period. It answers: *how well did the manager manage?* It strips out the effect of external cash flows.

cards.title: Time-weighted return
where: holding-period return of sub-period i, where a new sub-period starts at each external cash flow
cards.note: MWR: solve Σ CF_{t}/(1 + MWR)^{t} = 0, with deposits negative and withdrawals/ending value positive.

cards.title: Same investment, two answers
cards.body:
t0: buy 1 share at $100. t1: price $120, buy 1 more. t2: price $130, sell both ($260).

**TWR**: year 1 = 20%, year 2 = 8.33%. (1.20 × 1.0833)^{1/2} − 1 = **14.02%**.

**MWR**: cash flows −100, −120, +260 → IRR = **12.05%**.

MWR < TWR because more money was invested just before the weaker year.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: MWR is just FM's IRR applied to a portfolio. The new idea is TWR, the industry standard for judging managers because clients, not managers, control the timing of cash flows. If the manager controls the flows (e.g. private equity calls), MWR is appropriate.

cards.title: Index decisions
cards.body: To build an index you choose: the **target market**, the **constituents**, the **weighting** method, how often to **rebalance** (reset weights) and **reconstitute** (change members). A good benchmark is specified in advance, investable, measurable and reflects the manager's style.

cards.title: Weighting methods
rows: High-priced stocks dominate; splits change weights
Price × shares available to the public

cards.title: Price-weighted index
cards.note: After a split, change the divisor so the index value does not move: new divisor = new ΣP_{i} / old index value.

cards.title: Split adjustment
cards.body:
Three stocks priced 30, 60, 90; divisor 3 → index 60.

The $90 stock splits 3-for-1 → $30. New ΣP = 120.

New divisor = 120/60 = **2**. Index stays at 60, but the split stock's weight drops from 50% to 25%.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Market-cap weighting is self-rebalancing: weights move with prices, so no trading is needed. Equal weighting needs regular rebalancing because winners drift above 1/N.

cards.title: Index returns
cards.formula: Price return = Σ w_{i} × PR_{i} = (V_{1} − V_{0})/V_{0}        Total return = Σ w_{i} × TR_{i} = (V_{1} − V_{0} + income)/V_{0}
where: price and total return of constituent i
cards.note: A total-return index reinvests dividends/interest, so over time it grows faster than the price index.

cards.title: Same moves, three indexes
cards.body:
Start: A $50 (10m shares), B $20 (50m), C $100 (5m). End: A $55, B $18, C $110.

- Price-weighted: 183/170 − 1 = **+7.65%**
- Market-cap: caps 500+1,000+500 → 550+900+550: **0.00%**
- Equal-weighted: (10% − 10% + 10%)/3 = **+3.33%**

Weighting alone changes the benchmark's return.

cards.title: Price vs total return
cards.body:
Index starts at 1,000 and ends at 1,040; constituents paid income worth 15 index points.

Price return = 40/1,000 = **4.0%**.
Total return = (40 + 15)/1,000 = **5.5%**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A manager who receives and reinvests dividends should be compared with a *total-return* index. Comparing with a price index flatters the manager by the dividend yield.

questions.stem: An investor buys one share for $100. One year later the price is $120 and she buys a second share. At the end of year 2 the price is $130 and she sells both. Her annualized time-weighted return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Sub-period returns: 120/100 − 1 = 20% and 130/120 − 1 = 8.33%. TWR = (1.20 × 1.0833)^{1/2} − 1 = 1.30^{1/2} − 1 = 14.02%. 12.05% is the money-weighted return (IRR of −100, −120, +260). 30.00% is the cumulative 2-year return, not annualized.

questions.stem: Using the same facts (cash flows −100 at t0, −120 at t1, +260 at t2), the money-weighted return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Solve −100 − 120/(1 + r) + 260/(1 + r)^{2} = 0 → r = 12.05%. 14.02% is the TWR, and 8.33% is only the year-2 return. MWR is lower because more money was invested just before the weaker year.

questions.stem: A client adds large amounts to her account just before strong markets. The return that best evaluates the portfolio manager, who has no control over these flows, is the:
options: holding-period return of the client's total deposits
questions.explanation: TWR removes the effect of the size and timing of external cash flows, so it isolates the manager's decisions. The MWR would reward the manager for the client's lucky timing. A return on total deposits is also distorted by flow timing.

questions.stem: An investor makes a large deposit just before a period of poor returns. Compared with the time-weighted return, her money-weighted return will most likely be:
questions.explanation: MWR weights each period by the money invested. More money was exposed to the poor period, so MWR falls below TWR. They would be equal only with no intermediate cash flows.

questions.stem: In a price-weighted index of three stocks priced $30, $60 and $90, the divisor is 3. The $90 stock splits 3-for-1. The new divisor is closest to:
questions.explanation: Index before split = 180/3 = 60. After the split prices sum to 30 + 60 + 30 = 120. New divisor = 120/60 = 2.00, so the index stays at 60. Keeping 3 would drop the index to 40, and 1.00 would push it to 120.

questions.stem: Which weighting method requires the most frequent rebalancing to maintain its target weights?
questions.explanation: Equal weights drift as prices change, so the index must be rebalanced back to 1/N. Market-cap and price-weighted indexes adjust automatically with prices.

questions.stem: An index weights constituents by price × shares available to the public, excluding shares held by founders and governments. This is a:
questions.explanation: Using shares available for trading (the float) makes it float-adjusted market-cap weighting, which better reflects what investors can actually buy. Fundamental weighting uses accounting measures such as sales or earnings, and price weighting ignores share counts.

questions.stem: Stocks A, B and C start at $50, $20 and $100 with 10m, 50m and 5m shares outstanding. They end at $55, $18 and $110. The return of a market-cap-weighted index is closest to:
questions.explanation: Start caps: 500 + 1,000 + 500 = 2,000m. End: 550 + 900 + 550 = 2,000m. Return = 0.00%. 7.65% is the price-weighted return (183/170 − 1); 3.33% is the equal-weighted return.

questions.stem: An index starts at 1,000 and ends at 1,040. Constituents paid income equal to 15 index points. The total return is:
questions.explanation: Total return = (1,040 − 1,000 + 15)/1,000 = 5.5%. 4.0% is the price return only and 1.5% is only the income component.

questions.stem: A fund reinvests all dividends. The most appropriate benchmark is a:
options: price-weighted index regardless of return type
questions.explanation: Because the fund includes reinvested income, it must be compared with an index that does too. A price-return index omits dividends and makes the fund look better than it is.

questions.stem: An investor buys one share at $50. At the end of year 1 she receives a $2 dividend and buys another share at $55. At the end of year 2 she receives $2 per share and sells both shares at $60. Her money-weighted return is closest to:
A portfolio returns 5% in Q1, −3% from 1 April to 15 August (when the client withdraws cash), and 6% from 15 August to year-end. The time-weighted return for the year is closest to:
questions.explanation: Link sub-period returns: 1.05 × 0.97 × 1.06 − 1 = 7.96%. 8.00% adds the returns, and 2.67% is their simple average. The withdrawal only defines a sub-period break; it does not enter the TWR.

questions.stem: Stock prices: A $10 → $12, B $50 → $45, C $40 → $44. The return of a price-weighted index of these three stocks is closest to:
questions.explanation: Price-weighted: (12 + 45 + 44)/(10 + 50 + 40) − 1 = 101/100 − 1 = 1.00%. 6.67% is the equal-weighted average of +20%, −10% and +10%. −10.00% is only B's return; B moves the index most because it has the highest price, but it is not the whole index.

questions.stem: An index has beginning weights of 50%, 30% and 20% in stocks returning 8%, −2% and 5%. The index price return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Σw_{i}R_{i} = 0.5(8) + 0.3(−2) + 0.2(5) = 4.0 − 0.6 + 1.0 = 4.40%. 3.67% is the equal-weighted average and 11.00% simply adds the returns.

questions.stem: Which statement about a fundamentally weighted index is most accurate?
options: It tends to have a value tilt compared with a market-cap index
It tends to have a growth tilt compared with a market-cap index
Its weights are set equal to the price of each stock
questions.explanation: Weighting by sales, earnings or book value gives relatively more weight to firms with low price-to-fundamental ratios (value stocks) than market-cap weighting does. A growth tilt is the opposite, and weighting by price describes a price-weighted index.

flashcards.back: IRR of the investor's cash flows. Affected by timing and size of deposits and withdrawals. Measures the investor's experience.
Geometric linking of sub-period HPRs, split at each external cash flow, then annualized. Industry standard for evaluating managers.

flashcards.front: MWR vs TWR when money is added before a strong period
flashcards.back: MWR > TWR (more money earned the high return).

flashcards.front: Price-weighted index value and divisor after a split
flashcards.back: Index = ΣP_{i}/divisor. New divisor = post-split ΣP_{i} / pre-split index value.
Market-cap (and price) weighting: weights move with prices. Equal weighting must be rebalanced.

flashcards.front: Price return vs total return of an index

flashcards.back: Price: high-priced stocks dominate. Cap: large/overvalued firms dominate. Equal: small-cap tilt. Fundamental: value tilt.

modules.title: The Time Value of Money in Finance
modules.summary: Using present and future values to price bonds and equities, to back out implied returns and growth rates, and to apply cash-flow additivity and no-arbitrage to forward rates, FX forwards and option values.

acca.note: FM covered PV/FV, annuities, perpetuities, NPV/IRR, the dividend growth model and simple bond pricing and redemption yield. New for CFA: semiannual bond conventions, implied growth, continuous compounding, implied forward rates, FX forwards by no-arbitrage and one-period option replication.

lessons.title: TVM toolkit and the BA II Plus

cards.title: Future and present value
cards.note: Continuous compounding: FV = PV × e^{r_{s}×N}. EAR = (1 + r_{s}/m)^{m} − 1.

cards.title: Compounding frequency
cards.body:
$1,000 at 6% for 5 years:

- Annual: **$1,338.23**
- Monthly: 1,000 × 1.005^{60} = **$1,348.85**
- Continuous: 1,000 × e^{0.30} = **$1,349.86**

More frequent compounding → higher FV, with continuous as the upper limit.

cards.title: Annuities and perpetuities
cards.formula: PV_{annuity} = A × [1 − (1 + r)^{−N}] / r        PV_{perpetuity} = A / r
cards.note: Annuity due (payments at the start) = ordinary annuity × (1 + r). Growing perpetuity: PV = CF_{1}/(r − g).

cards.title: NPV and IRR on the cash-flow worksheet
cards.body:
Project: −1,000 now, then 300, 400, 500. Discount rate 8%.

NPV = **$17.63**; IRR = **8.90%**. NPV > 0 and IRR > 8% agree: accept.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The BA II Plus needs one negative and one positive among PV, PMT and FV, or it returns 'Error 5'. Keep P/Y = C/Y = 1 and enter the periodic rate and number of periods yourself; it avoids hidden-setting errors under exam pressure.

lessons.title: Pricing bonds and equities; implied return and growth

cards.title: Bond price
cards.note: Semiannual bond: halve the coupon and the yield, double the periods. Zero-coupon: P = F/(1 + r)^{N}.

cards.title: Bond pricing on the calculator
cards.body:
5-year, 6% annual coupon, face 100, YTM 7%: price **95.90** (discount, because coupon < yield).

Same bond paying semiannually: 10 periods, coupon 3, yield 3.5% → **95.84**.

cards.title: Equity: dividend models
cards.formula: Preferred / no growth: V_{0} = D/r        Constant growth: V_{0} = D_{1}/(r − g)
cards.note: Rearranged for implied values: r = D_{1}/P_{0} + g and g = r − D_{1}/P_{0}. Remember D_{1} = D_{0}(1 + g).

cards.title: Implied return and implied growth
cards.body:
Stock at $40, just paid $1.60, growth 5%: D_{1} = 1.68 → implied r = 1.68/40 + 5% = **9.2%**.

Stock at $50, next dividend $2, required return 10%: implied g = 10% − 2/50 = **6%**. The market price 'implies' these assumptions.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM's dividend valuation model is the same Gordon model, and FM's redemption yield is CFA's YTM. CFA adds semiannual conventions and the language of *implied* returns and growth: solving for r or g from a market price instead of a value. Watch D_{0} vs D_{1}.

cards.title: Cash-flow additivity
cards.body:
The PV of a stream equals the sum of the PVs of its parts. So two ways of getting the same future cash flows must cost the same today, otherwise there is an **arbitrage**: buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and lock in a riskless profit.

This single idea prices forward rates, FX forwards and options.

cards.title: FX forward by no-arbitrage
where: spot rate, price currency per 1 unit of base currency
cards.note: EUR/USD spot 1.10 (USD per EUR), r_{USD} 5%, r_{EUR} 3%, 1 year → F = 1.10 × 1.05/1.03 = 1.1214. The higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount.

cards.title: Pricing an option by replication
cards.body:
Stock $50 → $60 or $40 in one year; r_{f} 5%; call strike $50 pays $10 or $0.

Hedge ratio = (10 − 0)/(60 − 40) = 0.5. Buy 0.5 share ($25) and borrow 0.5 × 40/1.05 = $19.05. Payoffs match the call in both states.

Call value = 25 − 19.05 = **$5.95**.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM's interest-rate parity used the same F = S × (1 + r)/(1 + r) logic, but watch the quote: the rate of the currency in the **numerator (price currency)** goes on top. Option replication goes beyond AFM's Black–Scholes intro: it is pure no-arbitrage, with no probabilities of up/down needed.

questions.stem: $1,000 is invested at a stated annual rate of 6% compounded monthly for 5 years. The future value is closest to:
questions.explanation: FV = 1,000 × (1 + 0.06/12)^{60} = 1,348.85. $1,338.23 uses annual compounding and $1,349.86 uses continuous compounding.

questions.stem: A bank quotes 8% compounded quarterly. The effective annual rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: EAR = (1 + 0.08/4)^{4} − 1 = 8.24%. 8.00% is the stated rate, and 8.33% is the continuously compounded equivalent (e^{0.08} − 1).

questions.stem: An investor will receive $2,000 at the start of each year for 5 years. At a 7% discount rate, the present value is closest to:
questions.explanation: Payments at the start of each year form an annuity due: 8,200.39 × 1.07 = 8,774.42. $8,200.39 treats it as an ordinary annuity and $10,000 ignores discounting.

questions.stem: A project costs $1,000 and returns $300, $400 and $500 at the end of years 1–3. At a cost of capital of 8%, the NPV is closest to:
questions.explanation: NPV = −1,000 + 300/1.08 + 400/1.08^{2} + 500/1.08^{3} = 17.63. $200 ignores discounting, and the negative value has the sign reversed. The IRR is 8.90%, above 8%, consistent with a positive NPV.

questions.stem: A 5-year bond with a 6% annual coupon and $100 face value is priced to yield 7%. Its price is closest to:
questions.explanation: PV of 5 coupons of 6 plus 100 at 7% = 95.90. Because the coupon is below the yield, the bond trades at a discount. $100 would apply if yield = coupon, and $104.10 mirrors the discount into a premium.

questions.stem: A stock just paid a $2.00 dividend. Dividends are expected to grow at 4% forever and the required return is 9%. The value per share is closest to:
A stock trades at $50, its next annual dividend is expected to be $2.00 and investors require 10%. Under the constant-growth model, the implied growth rate is:
questions.explanation: g = r − D_{1}/P_{0} = 10% − 4% = 6.0%. 4.0% is the dividend yield, and 14.0% adds the yield to r instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: A 4-year bond with a 6% annual coupon trades at 104 per 100 face value. Its yield to maturity is closest to:
questions.explanation: Solve 4 [N], −104 [PV], 6 [PMT], 100 [FV], CPT [I/Y] → 4.88%. A premium bond's yield is below its coupon, so 6.00% is wrong. 5.77% is the current yield (6/104), which ignores the loss of the premium at maturity.

questions.stem: The 1-year spot rate is 3% and the 2-year spot rate is 4%. The implied 1-year forward rate one year from now is closest to:
questions.explanation: f_{1,1} = 1.04^{2}/1.03 − 1 = 5.01%. 5.00% is the arithmetic approximation (2 × 4 − 3), and 4.50% is the simple average of the two spot rates.

questions.stem: The EUR/USD spot rate is 1.1000 (USD per EUR). The 1-year USD rate is 5% and the EUR rate is 3%. The no-arbitrage 1-year forward rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: USD is the price currency, so F = 1.10 × 1.05/1.03 = 1.1214. 1.0790 puts the rates the wrong way round, and 1.1000 ignores the interest differential.

questions.stem: A stock at $50 will be worth $60 or $40 in one year. The risk-free rate is 5%. Using a replicating portfolio, the value of a 1-year call with a $50 strike is closest to:
questions.explanation: Hedge ratio = 10/20 = 0.5. Buy 0.5 share for $25 and borrow PV(20) = 19.05. Call = 25 − 19.05 = 5.95. $5.00 averages the payoffs without discounting or using the right probabilities, and $4.76 discounts that average (5/1.05).

questions.stem: A perpetuity pays $100 per year with the first payment at the end of year 4. At a 10% discount rate, its present value today is closest to:
questions.explanation: The perpetuity formula values it one period before the first payment: 100/0.10 = 1,000 at t = 3. Discount 3 years: 1,000/1.10^{3} = 751.31. $683.01 discounts 4 years, and $1,000 is the value at t = 3, not today.

questions.stem: An investor needs $500,000 in 20 years and can earn 6% per year. The equal end-of-year deposit required is closest to:
questions.explanation: Solve for PMT with FV = 500,000, N = 20, I/Y = 6: 13,592.28. $25,000 ignores interest (500,000/20). $43,592.28 wrongly treats the $500,000 as a PV to be repaid (PMT on a loan).

questions.stem: A $300,000 30-year mortgage at 6% has monthly payments. The payment is closest to:
questions.explanation: N = 360, I/Y = 0.5, PV = 300,000 → PMT = 1,798.65. $1,500 is interest only (300,000 × 0.005). $1,816.22 computes an annual payment (21,794.67) and divides it by 12, which ignores monthly compounding.

questions.stem: The 1-year spot rate is 3.0% and the 3-year spot rate is 4.5%. The implied 2-year forward rate starting in one year (annualized) is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1.045^{3}/1.03)^{1/2} − 1 = 5.26%. 5.25% is the arithmetic approximation (3 × 4.5 − 3)/2, and 6.00% is not supported by the spot rates.

questions.stem: A preferred share pays a fixed $4 annual dividend forever. If the required return is 7%, its value is closest to:
questions.explanation: No-growth perpetuity: 4/0.07 = 57.14. $28.00 multiplies instead of dividing. $61.14 adds a year's dividend to the value as if it were paid immediately.

flashcards.back: EAR = (1 + r_{s}/m)^{m} − 1; continuous: e^{r} − 1.
A × [1 − (1 + r)^{−N}]/r. Annuity due = ordinary × (1 + r).
V_{0} = D_{1}/(r − g), with D_{1} = D_{0}(1 + g). Requires r > g.
F = S × (1 + r_{price})^{T}/(1 + r_{base})^{T}, with S quoted as price currency per unit of base currency.
Hedge ratio = (c_{up} − c_{down})/(S_{up} − S_{down}). Call = hedge ratio × S_{0} − PV(borrowing).

flashcards.front: BA II Plus: switch to annuity due
flashcards.back: [2nd][BGN][2nd][SET][2nd][QUIT]. Display shows BGN.

modules.title: Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns
modules.summary: Describing a set of returns by its centre (mean, median, quantiles), its spread (variance, standard deviation, semi-deviation, coefficient of variation), its shape (skewness, kurtosis) and how two return series move together (covariance, correlation).

acca.note: MA/PM gave you the mean, standard deviation and perhaps the coefficient of variation. New for CFA: quantiles and box plots, target semi-deviation, skewness and kurtosis interpretation, and sample covariance/correlation with their pitfalls.

cards.title: Mean, median, mode
cards.body:
- **Mean**: the sum divided by count. Uses every value but is pulled by outliers.
- **Median**: the middle value of the sorted data (average the two middle values if n is even). Robust to outliers.
- **Mode**: the most frequent value or interval.

For returns 12, −4, 8, 15, −6, 9 (%): mean = **5.67%**, median = (8 + 9)/2 = **8.5%**.

cards.title: Locating a percentile
where: position of the y-th percentile in data sorted from low to high
cards.note: If L_{y} is not a whole number, interpolate between the neighbouring observations.

cards.title: Quartiles and the box plot
cards.body:
Sorted returns (n = 9): −8, −3, 1, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 18.

- Q1: L = 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 → −3 + 0.5 × (1 − (−3)) = **−1**
- Median: L = 5 → **6**
- Q3: L = 7.5 → 10 + 0.5 × 2 = **11**

Interquartile range = 11 − (−1) = **12**. A box plot draws Q1, the median and Q3 as a box, with whiskers to the extremes.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Quartiles split data into 4, quintiles into 5, deciles into 10, percentiles into 100. The 3rd quartile = 75th percentile. Watch the n + 1 in the location formula: using n is a classic distractor.

lessons.title: Dispersion: variance, standard deviation and downside risk

cards.title: Sample variance and standard deviation
cards.note: Divide by n − 1 for a sample (corrects bias); by N for a whole population. MAD = Σ|X_{i} − X̄|/n; range = max − min.

cards.title: Using the STAT worksheet
cards.body:
Returns 12, −4, 8, 15, −6, 9 (%).

Mean 5.67, sample SD **8.64**, population SD 7.89, MAD 7.11, range 21.

cards.title: Target semi-deviation
cards.note: Only observations at or below the target count in the numerator, but divide by the full n − 1.

cards.title: Downside risk
cards.body:
Same returns, target B = 0%. Below-target values: −4 and −6.

s_{target} = √[(16 + 36)/5] = √10.4 = **3.22%**.

With a target of 2%: √[(36 + 64)/5] = **4.47%**. A higher target means more downside risk.

cards.title: Coefficient of variation
cards.note: Risk per unit of return. Lower CV = better risk-return trade-off. Meaningless when the mean is near zero or negative.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: You know SD and CV from MA/PM. New: the n − 1 sample divisor (the BA II Plus shows both Sx and σx; exam questions about historical samples want Sx) and semi-deviation, which captures only the downside that investors actually dislike.

cards.title: Shape of a distribution
rows: Long right tail; mean > median > mode
Long left tail; mean < median < mode
> 0: leptokurtic, fat tails, more extreme outcomes

cards.title: Why shape matters for investors
cards.body:
Normal distribution: skewness 0, kurtosis 3 (excess kurtosis 0). Many asset returns are **negatively skewed and leptokurtic**: frequent small gains, occasional large losses. Using only mean and SD then **understates** the chance of a crash.

Investors prefer positive skew (lottery-like upside).

cards.title: Sample covariance and correlation
cards.note: Covariance has squared units and no bounds; correlation is unit-free and lies between −1 and +1.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Correlation measures only **linear** association: r = 0 does not mean no relationship. It is sensitive to outliers, and a high r can be **spurious** (chance, or both series driven by a third variable). Correlation never proves causation.

questions.stem: For the returns 12%, −4%, 8%, 15%, −6% and 9%, the median is:
questions.explanation: Sorted: −6, −4, 8, 9, 12, 15. With n even, the median is the average of the two middle values: (8 + 9)/2 = 8.50%. 5.67% is the mean, and 8.00% takes only one middle value.

questions.stem: Nine returns sorted from lowest to highest are −8, −3, 1, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 18 (%). The third quartile is closest to:
questions.explanation: L_{75} = (9 + 1) × 0.75 = 7.5 → halfway between the 7th (10) and 8th (12) observations = 11.0%. 10.0% and 12.0% each take one neighbouring observation instead of interpolating between them.

questions.stem: A return series has a few extreme negative outliers. Which measure of central tendency is least affected by them?
questions.explanation: The median depends only on the middle of the sorted data, so a few extreme values barely move it. The arithmetic and geometric means both use every value, so large negative outliers drag them down.

questions.stem: For returns of 12%, −4%, 8%, 15%, −6% and 9%, the sample standard deviation is closest to:
questions.explanation: Mean 5.67; Σ(X − X̄)^{2} = 373.33; s^{2} = 373.33/5 = 74.67; s = 8.64%. 7.89% divides by n (population SD) and 74.67 is the variance (in %^{2}), not the SD.
questions.calc: [2nd][DATA] enter the six values, [2nd][STAT] 1-V: Sx = 8.64, σx = 7.89

questions.stem: Using the same six returns (12, −4, 8, 15, −6, 9 %) and a target return of 0%, the target semi-deviation is closest to:
questions.explanation: Only −4 and −6 are below target: √[(16 + 36)/(6 − 1)] = √10.4 = 3.22%. 2.94% divides by n = 6. 6.78% uses the mean as the target instead of 0%.

questions.stem: Fund A: mean return 8%, SD 12%. Fund B: mean return 5%, SD 6%. Based on the coefficient of variation, which is correct?
options: Fund A has less risk per unit of return
Fund B has less risk per unit of return
Both funds have the same risk per unit of return
questions.explanation: CV_{A} = 12/8 = 1.5 and CV_{B} = 6/5 = 1.2. The lower CV (Fund B) means less risk per unit of return. Looking only at mean return favours A, which is the trap.

questions.stem: A return distribution has mean 4%, median 6% and mode 7%. It is most likely:
questions.explanation: Mean < median < mode signals a long left tail: negative skew. Positive skew would have mean > median > mode, and a symmetric distribution would have all three equal.

questions.stem: A return distribution has excess kurtosis of 1.8. Compared with a normal distribution, it most likely has:
options: fatter tails, so extreme returns are more likely
thinner tails, so extreme returns are less likely
the same tails but a negative skew
questions.explanation: Positive excess kurtosis means leptokurtic: more probability in the tails (and peak) than the normal. Thinner tails would need negative excess kurtosis, and kurtosis says nothing about skew.

questions.stem: The covariance between two stocks' returns is 0.012. Their standard deviations are 20% and 10%. Their correlation is closest to:
questions.explanation: r = 0.012/(0.20 × 0.10) = 0.60. 0.06 divides by the 20% SD only and 0.12 divides by the 10% SD only. Always divide covariance by the product of both standard deviations.

questions.stem: For the returns 12, −4, 8, 15, −6 and 9 (%), the target semi-deviation with a 2% target is closest to:
questions.explanation: Below-target returns: −4 and −6 → deviations from 2 are −6 and −8. √[(36 + 64)/5] = √20 = 4.47%. 3.22% uses a 0% target, and 4.08% divides by n = 6 (√(100/6)).

questions.stem: Which statement about correlation is most accurate?
options: Two variables can show high correlation without any causal link
A correlation of zero means the two variables are unrelated in every way
questions.explanation: Spurious correlation arises by chance or through a third variable, so high r does not imply causation. r = 0 rules out only a linear relationship, and outliers can distort r substantially.

questions.stem: Five annual returns are 3%, −1%, 5%, 7% and 1%. The mean absolute deviation is closest to:
questions.explanation: Mean = 3. Absolute deviations: 0, 4, 2, 4, 2 → sum 12; MAD = 12/5 = 2.40%. 3.16% is the sample SD and 2.83% the population SD.

questions.stem: An analyst compares two hedge-fund strategies with equal mean and standard deviation. Strategy X has negative skew and excess kurtosis of 3; Strategy Y has positive skew and excess kurtosis near 0. A risk-averse investor would most likely prefer:
options: Strategy X, because its higher kurtosis means more consistent returns
either strategy, because mean and SD are identical
Strategy Y, because it has less exposure to large losses
questions.explanation: With equal mean and SD, investors prefer positive skew and thinner tails. X's negative skew and fat tails mean a greater chance of large losses. Mean and SD alone miss these differences, so they are not equivalent.

questions.stem: Four paired observations are X: 5, 10, −2, 7 and Y: 3, 8, 1, 4. The sample covariance is closest to:
questions.explanation: X̄ = 5, Ȳ = 4. Cross-products: 0 × (−1) + 5 × 4 + (−7)(−3) + 2 × 0 = 41. s_{XY} = 41/(4 − 1) = 13.67. 10.25 divides by n = 4, and 0.91 is the correlation.

flashcards.back: s^{2} = Σ(X_{i} − X̄)^{2}/(n − 1). Population divides by N.
L_{y} = (n + 1) × y/100; interpolate if not a whole number.
√[Σ_{X ≤ B}(X_{i} − B)^{2}/(n − 1)]: only below-target observations, but divide by full n − 1.
CV = s/X̄; risk per unit of return. Lower is better.
Positive: mean > median > mode, long right tail. Negative: mean < median < mode, long left tail.
Leptokurtic: fatter tails than normal; extreme outcomes more likely.
r = s_{XY}/(s_{X}s_{Y}); −1 to +1; linear only; sensitive to outliers; not causation.

flashcards.front: BA II Plus: sample vs population SD
flashcards.back: STAT worksheet 1-V shows Sx (sample, n − 1) and σx (population, n).

modules.title: Statistical Distributions for Financial Asset Prices and Returns
modules.summary: Expected values, variances and covariances from probability-weighted scenarios, conditional expectations with probability trees, Bayesian updating, and the key distributions used in finance: binomial, normal, lognormal, t, chi-square and F.

acca.note: MA/PM taught expected values and decision trees. New for CFA: variance and covariance across scenarios, conditional expectations and variances, Bayes' formula, and the properties of the normal, lognormal, t, χ² and F distributions.

lessons.title: Expected value, variance and covariance from scenarios

cards.title: Expected value and variance
cards.note: Covariance of two assets: Cov(A, B) = Σ P(s)[R_{A,s} − E(R_{A})][R_{B,s} − E(R_{B})].

cards.title: Total probability rule for expectations
cards.note: Extends to any set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive scenarios. A probability tree is just this rule drawn as branches.

cards.title: Probability tree for EPS
cards.body:
Rates fall (0.4): EPS 2.80 or 2.20 (50/50) → E(EPS | fall) = 2.50.
Rates stable (0.6): EPS 2.30 (0.25) or 1.90 (0.75) → E(EPS | stable) = 2.00.

Unconditional E(EPS) = 0.4 × 2.50 + 0.6 × 2.00 = **2.20**.

Conditional variances: 0.09 (fall), 0.03 (stable). Unconditional variance over the four end-nodes = **0.114**.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: PM's expected values and decision trees carry over directly. New: CFA asks for the **variance** and **covariance** across scenarios, and conditional expectations that change as information arrives. Probabilities are weights; never divide by n here.

cards.title: Bayes' formula
cards.formula: P(Event | Info) = P(Info | Event) × P(Event) / P(Info)
where: likelihood of seeing the information if the event is true
unconditional probability of the information (total probability rule)
cards.note: Result = updated (posterior) probability.

cards.title: Dividend-cut signal
cards.body:
30% of firms in a sector will cut dividends. A warning signal appears for 80% of cutters and 20% of non-cutters.

P(signal) = 0.3 × 0.8 + 0.7 × 0.2 = 0.24 + 0.14 = 0.38.

P(cut | signal) = 0.24/0.38 = **63.2%**.

The signal more than doubles the 30% prior, but it is far from certain.

cards.title: A table beats the formula
cards.body:
Under time pressure, imagine 1,000 cases:

- 300 cutters → 240 signal
- 700 non-cutters → 140 signal

Of 380 signals, 240 are cutters: 240/380 = 63.2%. Same answer, fewer chances to slip.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: The classic error is answering with P(Info | Event) (80%) instead of P(Event | Info) (63.2%). Another: forgetting false positives from the large non-event group in the denominator.

cards.title: Binomial distribution
cards.note: Mean = np, variance = np(1 − p). Each trial is a Bernoulli (success/failure) with constant p and independent trials.

cards.title: Binomial in action
cards.body:
A stock rises in any month with p = 0.6, independently. Over 5 months:

P(exactly 3 up) = 10 × 0.6^{3} × 0.4^{2} = **0.3456**.
P(at least 3 up) = 0.3456 + 0.2592 + 0.0778 = **0.6826**.

Mean = 5 × 0.6 = 3 up-months; variance = 1.2.

cards.title: Normal distribution and z
cards.note: About 68% of outcomes lie within ±1σ, 90% within ±1.645σ, 95% within ±1.96σ, 99% within ±2.58σ.

cards.title: Other distributions
rows: Asset prices (if log returns are normal)
Symmetric, fatter tails than normal; approaches normal as df rises
Test of equal variances; regression F-test

questions.stem: Returns on Asset A are 20%, 10% and −10% with probabilities 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2. The standard deviation of A's return is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(A) = 9%. Variance = 0.3(11)^{2} + 0.5(1)^{2} + 0.2(−19)^{2} = 36.3 + 0.5 + 72.2 = 109 (%^{2}); SD = √109 = 10.44%. 109 is the variance, not the SD. 12.47% treats the three outcomes as equally likely (dividing squared deviations from their simple mean by 3), ignoring the probabilities.

questions.stem: In scenarios with probabilities 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2, Asset A returns 20%, 10%, −10% and Asset B returns 5%, 8%, 12%. The covariance between A and B (in %^{2}) is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(A) = 9, E(B) = 7.9. Cov = 0.3(11)(−2.9) + 0.5(1)(0.1) + 0.2(−19)(4.1) = −9.57 + 0.05 − 15.58 = −25.1. The positive value has the wrong sign: A and B move in opposite directions. −8.4 divides the covariance by 3 as if it were a simple average; the probabilities already do the weighting.

questions.stem: If interest rates fall (probability 0.4) a firm's expected EPS is $2.50; otherwise its expected EPS is $2.00. The unconditional expected EPS is:
questions.explanation: Total probability rule: 0.4 × 2.50 + 0.6 × 2.00 = 1.00 + 1.20 = $2.20. $2.25 is the unweighted average. $2.30 reverses the probabilities (0.6 × 2.50 + 0.4 × 2.00).

questions.stem: Which statement about conditional expected values is most accurate?
options: They are fixed once a variable's distribution is known
They are updated as new information about scenarios becomes available
They always equal the unconditional expected value
questions.explanation: A conditional expectation is the expected value given a scenario or piece of information, so it changes as information changes. It equals the unconditional expectation only if the information is irrelevant.

questions.stem: 30% of firms in a sector will cut their dividend. A warning signal appears for 80% of firms that cut and for 20% of firms that do not. Given a signal, the probability that a firm will cut its dividend is closest to:
questions.explanation: P(signal) = 0.3 × 0.8 + 0.7 × 0.2 = 0.38. P(cut | signal) = 0.24/0.38 = 63.2%. 80% is P(signal | cut), the inverse probability. 24% is the joint probability P(cut and signal).

questions.stem: 20% of fund managers are skilled. A skilled manager beats the index in a given year with probability 0.7; an unskilled one with probability 0.4. A manager beats the index this year. The probability that she is skilled is closest to:
questions.explanation: P(beat) = 0.2 × 0.7 + 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.14 + 0.32 = 0.46. P(skilled | beat) = 0.14/0.46 = 30.4%. 20% is the unchanged prior, and 70% is P(beat | skilled).

questions.stem: In Bayes' formula, the updated probability of an event after new information is called the:
questions.explanation: Bayes converts a prior probability into a posterior (updated) probability using the likelihood of the information. The unconditional probability of the information is the denominator.

questions.stem: A stock rises in any month with probability 0.6, independently of other months. The probability that it rises in exactly 3 of the next 5 months is closest to:
questions.explanation: P = C(5,3) × 0.6^{3} × 0.4^{2} = 10 × 0.216 × 0.16 = 0.3456. 0.2160 omits the 10 combinations and the down-months, and 0.6000 is just p.

questions.stem: Annual returns are normally distributed with mean 8% and standard deviation 12%. The range that contains about 95% of outcomes is closest to:
Which distribution is most appropriate for modelling a stock's price, given that its continuously compounded returns are normally distributed?
questions.explanation: If ln(S_{T}/S_{0}) is normal, S_{T} is lognormal: right-skewed and never negative, like real prices. A normal distribution allows negative prices, and the t-distribution is used for small-sample inference.

questions.stem: Compared with the standard normal distribution, a Student's t-distribution with 10 degrees of freedom has:
questions.explanation: The t-distribution is symmetric with fatter tails, reflecting extra uncertainty from estimating σ; it converges to the normal as df rises. It is not skewed.

questions.stem: An economy is in expansion, normal or recession with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. A leading indicator turns positive with probability 0.8, 0.5 and 0.1 in those states. Given a positive reading, the probability of expansion is closest to:
questions.explanation: P(positive) = 0.5(0.8) + 0.3(0.5) + 0.2(0.1) = 0.40 + 0.15 + 0.02 = 0.57. P(expansion | positive) = 0.40/0.57 = 70.2%. 50% is the prior, and 80% is P(positive | expansion).

questions.stem: Annual returns are normally distributed with mean 8% and standard deviation 12%. The probability of a negative return is closest to:
questions.explanation: z = (0 − 8)/12 = −0.67; N(−0.67) ≈ 0.25. 16% is the probability of a return below −4% (z = −1). 33% is not supported by the normal table.

questions.stem: A firm's EPS outcomes are $2.80 (probability 0.20), $2.20 (0.20), $2.30 (0.15) and $1.90 (0.45). The standard deviation of EPS is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(EPS) = 0.56 + 0.44 + 0.345 + 0.855 = 2.20. Variance = 0.2(0.6)^{2} + 0.2(0)^{2} + 0.15(0.1)^{2} + 0.45(−0.3)^{2} = 0.072 + 0 + 0.0015 + 0.0405 = 0.114; SD = 0.338. 0.114 is the variance, not the SD. 0.374 ignores the probabilities and computes a sample SD of the four outcomes (dividing by n − 1 = 3).

questions.stem: A stock priced at 100 moves up 10% (probability 0.6) or down 10% each period, independently. The probability that it is at 99 after two periods is closest to:
questions.explanation: A price of 99 needs one up and one down move (100 × 1.1 × 0.9), which can happen in 2 orders: 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. 0.24 counts only one path, and 0.36 is the probability of two up moves.

flashcards.back: σ^{2} = Σ P(s)[X_{s} − E(X)]^{2}: probability-weighted, no n − 1.
E(X) = Σ E(X | S_{i}) × P(S_{i}) for mutually exclusive, exhaustive scenarios.
P(Event | Info) = P(Info | Event) × P(Event)/P(Info).
Mean = np; variance = np(1 − p).
Right-skewed, bounded below by 0. Asset prices are lognormal if continuously compounded returns are normal.
t is symmetric with fatter tails; defined by df; approaches the normal as df rises.
Both non-negative and right-skewed. χ²: one df, tests a variance. F: two df, tests a ratio of variances.

modules.title: Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
modules.summary: From samples to conclusions: sampling methods, the central limit theorem, standard errors and confidence intervals, then the hypothesis-testing process, errors and power, and the main parametric and non-parametric tests.

acca.note: Hypothesis testing is new: ACCA covers descriptive statistics but not formal inference. Expect several exam questions on choosing the right test statistic and degrees of freedom and on interpreting p-values.

lessons.title: Sampling, the CLT and confidence intervals

cards.title: Sampling methods
rows: Random draws within subgroups in proportion to their size
Bond index replication by sector/duration; smaller error

cards.title: Central limit theorem (CLT)
cards.body:
For a large sample (n ≥ 30 rule of thumb), the **sample mean** is approximately normal, whatever the population's distribution, with mean μ and variance σ^{2}/n.

This is why we can build z- and t-based confidence intervals for mean returns even though returns are not normal. **Sampling error** = sample statistic − population parameter.

cards.title: Standard error and confidence interval
cards.formula: σ_{X̄} = σ/√n  (or s/√n)        CI = X̄ ± reliability factor × standard error
cards.note: Reliability factor: z (σ known, or large sample) or t with n − 1 df (σ unknown). 90%: 1.645; 95%: 1.96; 99%: 2.58.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Bigger n → smaller SE → narrower interval. Higher confidence → wider interval. **Bootstrap** resamples the observed data *with replacement* many times to estimate a standard error; **jackknife** re-estimates the statistic leaving out one observation at a time.

lessons.title: The hypothesis-testing process, errors and p-values

cards.title: The steps
cards.body:
1. State H_{0} (always contains =, ≤ or ≥) and H_{a}.
2. Choose the test statistic and its distribution.
3. Set the significance level α.
4. Find the critical value(s).
5. Compute the statistic, compare, and **reject or fail to reject H_{0}**.
6. Make the economic/investment decision.

We never 'accept' H_{0}. Put the claim you want to prove in H_{a}.

cards.title: p-values
cards.body:
The **p-value** is the smallest significance level at which H_{0} can be rejected. Rule: **reject if p-value < α**.

p = 0.03 → reject at 5% and 10%, not at 1%.

Two-tailed (H_{a}: μ ≠ μ_{0}) splits α between both tails; one-tailed (H_{a}: μ > μ_{0}) puts all of α in one tail, so its critical value is smaller in absolute terms (1.645 vs 1.96 at 5%).

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Lowering α (say 5% → 1%) cuts Type I error but **raises** Type II error and lowers power, for the same n. Only a bigger sample reduces both. Also: statistically significant is not the same as economically significant (after costs and taxes the edge may vanish).

cards.title: A t-test that just misses
cards.body:
25 monthly alphas: mean 1.2%, s 3%. H_{0}: μ = 0 vs H_{a}: μ ≠ 0 at 5%.

t = 1.2/(3/√25) = **2.00**. Critical t_{0.025, 24} = 2.064 → **fail to reject**.

One-tailed (H_{a}: μ > 0): critical 1.711 → reject. The tail choice matters.

cards.title: Non-parametric tests
cards.body:
Use when data are ranks, the distribution assumptions fail (e.g. small, non-normal samples, outliers), or the hypothesis is not about a parameter.

**Spearman rank correlation**: r_{s} = 1 − 6Σd^{2}/[n(n^{2} − 1)], where d = difference in ranks. Example: n = 5, Σd^{2} = 4 → r_{s} = 1 − 24/120 = **0.80**.

Other examples: sign test, Wilcoxon, Mann–Whitney.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Paired test = same subjects measured twice or two series sharing the same dates (dependent). Pooled t = two independent samples with equal variances. Getting this choice right is a frequent question.

questions.stem: A sample of 64 observations has a mean of 9% and a standard deviation of 20%. The 95% confidence interval for the population mean is closest to:
questions.explanation: SE = 20/√64 = 2.5. CI = 9 ± 1.96 × 2.5 = 4.1% to 13.9%. 4.9% to 13.1% uses the 90% factor (1.645). −30.2% to 48.2% uses the SD instead of the standard error.

questions.stem: The central limit theorem states that, for a large sample, the distribution of the sample mean is:
options: normal only if the population is normal
approximately normal, regardless of the population's distribution
questions.explanation: The CLT says the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and variance σ^{2}/n for large n, even when the population is not normal. It does not require the population to be normal, and the sample mean's distribution is not the population's distribution (its variance is σ^{2}/n, not σ^{2}).

questions.stem: An analyst divides a bond index into cells by sector and maturity and randomly selects bonds from each cell in proportion to its index weight. This is:
questions.explanation: Random selection within each subgroup, in proportion to its size, is stratified random sampling. Cluster sampling picks whole groups at random, and convenience sampling is not random at all.

questions.stem: A sample of 16 returns has mean 10% and standard deviation 8%. The population variance is unknown. The 95% confidence interval for the mean is closest to:
questions.explanation: σ unknown and n small → use t with 15 df: 2.131. SE = 8/4 = 2. CI = 10 ± 4.26 = 5.74% to 14.26%. 6.08% to 13.92% wrongly uses z = 1.96, and the wide interval uses the SD instead of the SE.

questions.stem: A Type I error occurs when an analyst:
options: fails to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: Type I = rejecting a true H_{0}; its probability is α. Failing to reject a false H_{0} is a Type II error, and rejecting a false H_{0} is the correct decision (power).

questions.stem: A test of whether a fund's mean alpha differs from zero gives a p-value of 0.03. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Reject H_{0} at the 5% level but not at the 1% level
Reject H_{0} at both the 1% and 5% levels
Fail to reject H_{0} at the 5% level
questions.explanation: Reject when p < α: 0.03 < 0.05 (reject) but 0.03 > 0.01 (fail to reject). Rejecting at 1% would need p < 0.01, and failing to reject at 5% would need p ≥ 0.05.

questions.stem: Holding the sample size constant, reducing the significance level from 5% to 1% will most likely:
options: reduce the probability of a Type II error
increase the probability of a Type II error
increase the power of the test
questions.explanation: A stricter α makes rejection harder, so false nulls are rejected less often: β (Type II) rises and power (1 − β) falls. Only a larger sample can reduce both error types together.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to show that a strategy's mean return is greater than 2%. The correct hypotheses are:
questions.explanation: The claim to be supported goes in H_{a}, and H_{0} holds the equality. So H_{0}: μ ≤ 2% vs H_{a}: μ > 2%, a one-tailed test. Putting μ > 2% in H_{0} reverses them, and μ = 2% vs μ ≠ 2% is a two-tailed test that does not match a directional claim.

questions.stem: 25 monthly alphas have a mean of 1.2% and a standard deviation of 3%. Testing H_{0}: μ = 0 against H_{a}: μ ≠ 0 at the 5% level (critical t = 2.064), the analyst should:
options: fail to reject H_{0}, because t = 2.00 is below 2.064
questions.explanation: t = 1.2/(3/√25) = 1.2/0.6 = 2.00 < 2.064 → fail to reject. Comparing with the z value 1.96 is wrong when σ is estimated from a small sample. t = 10.00 divides s by n instead of √n (1.2/(3/25)).

questions.stem: An analyst compares the mean returns of the same 36 stocks before and after an index inclusion. The most appropriate test is a:
options: chi-square test of a single variance
questions.explanation: The same stocks are measured twice, so the samples are dependent: use the paired comparisons test on the differences (df = n − 1). The pooled t-test assumes independent samples, and χ² tests a variance, not a mean.

questions.stem: A sample correlation of 0.40 is calculated from 27 observations. The t-statistic for testing H_{0}: ρ = 0 is closest to:
questions.explanation: t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r^{2}) = 0.4 × 5/√0.84 = 2.18. 2.00 omits the √(1 − r^{2}) term, and 2.38 divides by (1 − r^{2}) = 0.84 without taking the square root. df = 25.

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly calls for a non-parametric test?
options: Testing the correlation between two variables measured only as ranks
Testing whether a large sample's mean return differs from zero
Testing whether a normally distributed population's variance equals 4%
questions.explanation: Ranked data do not support parametric assumptions, so a test such as Spearman rank correlation is appropriate. A large-sample mean test relies on the CLT (parametric t/z), and a variance test on a normal population uses χ².

questions.stem: A sample of 21 monthly returns has a standard deviation of 12%. An analyst tests H_{0}: σ ≤ 10% against H_{a}: σ > 10% at the 5% level. The upper critical value of χ² with 20 df is 31.41. The test statistic and decision are:
questions.explanation: χ² = (n − 1)s^{2}/σ_{0}^{2} = 20 × 144/100 = 28.8 < 31.41 → fail to reject. 30.2 wrongly uses n = 21 instead of n − 1. Rejecting would require the statistic to exceed the critical value.

questions.stem: Two independent samples give s_{1} = 15% (n = 31) and s_{2} = 10% (n = 25). Testing equality of variances at the 5% level (two-tailed), the upper critical F(30, 24) value is 2.21. The analyst should:
questions.explanation: F = s_{1}^{2}/s_{2}^{2} = 225/100 = 2.25 (larger variance on top) > 2.21 → reject equal variances. 1.50 uses the ratio of SDs instead of variances, and 0.44 puts the smaller variance on top.

questions.stem: Paired differences between two strategies' monthly returns over 36 months have a mean of 0.5% and a standard deviation of 1.5%. The t-statistic for H_{0}: μ_{d} = 0 is closest to:
questions.explanation: s_{d̄} = 1.5/√36 = 0.25; t = 0.5/0.25 = 2.00 with 35 df. 0.33 divides by s_{d} instead of the standard error, and 12.00 multiplies by √n twice.

questions.stem: Two analysts each rank the same five stocks, and the sum of squared rank differences is Σd^{2} = 4. The Spearman rank correlation is closest to:
A researcher finds that a trading rule produces a statistically significant mean excess return at the 1% level. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The rule must be economically profitable
The result proves the null hypothesis is false
The rule may still be unprofitable after transaction costs and taxes
questions.explanation: Statistical significance does not guarantee economic significance: costs, taxes and risk can wipe out a small but significant edge. Hypothesis tests never prove anything with certainty; a 1% Type I error risk remains.

flashcards.front: Standard error of the sample mean
flashcards.back: σ/√n (or s/√n when σ is unknown).

flashcards.front: Type I vs Type II error
flashcards.back: Type I: reject a true H_{0} (prob. α). Type II: fail to reject a false H_{0} (prob. β). Power = 1 − β.
Reject H_{0} if p-value < α.

flashcards.front: Test statistic for a single variance

flashcards.back: r_{s} = 1 − 6Σd^{2}/[n(n^{2} − 1)]; non-parametric.

modules.title: The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
modules.summary: How weights, variances and correlations combine into portfolio risk and return, how to find the minimum-variance portfolio and the efficient frontier, and how a risk-free asset and investor risk aversion lead to the capital allocation line, the optimal portfolio and the capital market line.

acca.note: AFM covered two-asset portfolio risk and the efficient frontier; FM covered CAPM and diversification. New for CFA: the global minimum-variance weight formula, mean-variance utility U = E(R) − ½Aσ², and choosing the optimal point on the CAL.

cards.title: Two-asset portfolio
cards.note: N assets: σ_{p}^{2} = ΣΣ w_{i}w_{j}Cov_{ij}. With many assets, covariances, not individual variances, drive portfolio risk.

cards.title: Key relationships
cards.body:
- Return is a weighted average; risk is **not** (unless ρ = +1).
- Lower correlation → lower portfolio σ for the same expected return.
- With ρ = −1 a zero-risk portfolio exists.
- Adding assets removes diversifiable (unsystematic) risk; market (systematic) risk remains.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Convert to decimals before squaring (0.20^{2} = 0.04) and remember the factor of 2 on the covariance term. If given covariance directly, do not multiply by σ_{1}σ_{2} again.

lessons.title: Minimum-variance portfolio and the efficient frontier

cards.title: Global minimum-variance (GMV) weight, two assets
cards.note: w_{2}^{*} = 1 − w_{1}^{*}. The GMV portfolio has the lowest possible risk of any combination.

cards.title: Efficient frontier
cards.body:
Plot every risky portfolio in σ–E(R) space: the outer curve is the **minimum-variance frontier**. The part **above** the GMV portfolio is the **efficient frontier**: highest return for each level of risk.

Portfolios below the GMV point are inefficient: another portfolio gives more return for the same risk.

cards.title: Python PSM link
cards.body: The 2027 Python practical skills module builds this numerically: compute a covariance matrix from return data, then search weights to minimise σ_{p} for each target return. The two-asset formula is the hand-calculated version you need for the exam.

lessons.title: Risk aversion, the CAL and the CML

cards.title: Mean-variance utility
where: risk-aversion coefficient (higher = more risk averse; 0 = risk neutral; < 0 = risk seeking)

cards.title: Capital allocation line (CAL)
cards.note: Combining the risk-free asset with the risky portfolio gives a straight line. The best CAL is tangent to the efficient frontier.

cards.title: From CAL to CML
cards.body:
If all investors share the same expectations, they all hold the **same** tangency portfolio, which must be the **market portfolio**. The CAL becomes the **capital market line (CML)**.

Investors differ only in how much they lend or borrow (**two-fund separation**): risk aversion sets the mix, not the risky portfolio.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: AFM showed the CML and CAPM. New here: the utility function with A, the optimal-weight formula, and indifference curves. A more risk-averse investor (higher A) has steeper indifference curves and sits closer to R_{f} on the same CAL.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds 60% in A (E = 10%, σ = 20%) and 40% in B (E = 6%, σ = 10%). The correlation is 0.3. The portfolio standard deviation is closest to:
Holding weights and individual risks constant, a decrease in the correlation between two assets will:
questions.explanation: Lower correlation shrinks the covariance term, so portfolio risk falls. Expected return is a weighted average of asset returns and does not depend on correlation.

questions.stem: Two assets with σ of 20% and 10% are perfectly negatively correlated. A portfolio of 60% and 40% respectively has a standard deviation of:
questions.explanation: With ρ = −1, σ_{p} = |w_{1}σ_{1} − w_{2}σ_{2}| = |12% − 4%| = 8%. 16% assumes ρ = +1. Zero risk requires the specific weights 1/3 and 2/3, not 60/40.

questions.stem: Asset 1 has σ = 20% and Asset 2 has σ = 10%; their covariance is 0.006. The weight of Asset 1 in the global minimum-variance portfolio is closest to:
The efficient frontier is best described as the:
options: set of all portfolios with the lowest risk for each level of return
portion of the minimum-variance frontier above the global minimum-variance portfolio
line from the risk-free rate to the market portfolio
questions.explanation: Efficient portfolios offer the highest return for each level of risk, which is the upper part of the minimum-variance frontier starting at the GMV point. The whole minimum-variance frontier includes inefficient portfolios below the GMV, and the line from R_{f} is the CAL/CML.

questions.stem: A portfolio lies on the minimum-variance frontier but below the global minimum-variance portfolio. It is:
options: efficient, because it has minimum variance for its return
the optimal portfolio for a highly risk-averse investor
inefficient, because another portfolio offers a higher return for the same risk
questions.explanation: For any portfolio below the GMV, a portfolio on the upper branch has the same σ and a higher return, so it is inefficient. Even the most risk-averse investor would choose the GMV (or a mix with R_{f}) instead.

questions.stem: An investor with a risk-aversion coefficient of 4 compares Portfolio X (E = 10%, σ = 20%) and Portfolio Y (E = 7%, σ = 10%). Which statement is correct?
options: Y has the higher utility, 0.05 vs 0.02
X has the higher utility, 0.02 vs 0.05
questions.explanation: U_{X} = 0.10 − 0.5 × 4 × 0.04 = 0.02; U_{Y} = 0.07 − 0.5 × 4 × 0.01 = 0.05. Y is preferred. Equal utility of 0.06 would apply for A = 2.

questions.stem: R_{f} = 3%. The tangency portfolio has an expected return of 9% and σ of 15%. A portfolio on the CAL with σ = 12% has an expected return closest to:
questions.explanation: Sharpe = (9 − 3)/15 = 0.40; E = 3 + 0.40 × 12 = 7.8%. 7.2% is 80% of 9% (forgetting the 20% in R_{f}). 10.2% adds R_{f} to 80% of 9%, double-counting the risk-free component.

questions.stem: If investors have homogeneous expectations, the capital allocation line that all of them use is the:
questions.explanation: Identical expectations → everyone holds the same tangency portfolio = market portfolio, so the shared CAL is the CML. The SML plots return against beta (CAPM), and the minimum-variance frontier contains only risky assets.

questions.stem: Compared with a less risk-averse investor facing the same CAL, a more risk-averse investor will most likely:
options: hold the same risky portfolio but a larger allocation to the risk-free asset
hold a different risky portfolio with lower-volatility stocks
hold the same allocation to the risk-free asset
questions.explanation: Two-fund separation: all investors hold the same tangency portfolio; risk aversion only determines the split between it and R_{f}. A more risk-averse investor lends more.

questions.stem: Asset A: σ = 25%; Asset B: σ = 15%; correlation 0.3. The weight of A in the global minimum-variance portfolio is closest to:
An investor has A = 4. R_{f} = 3% and the optimal risky portfolio has E(R) = 9% and σ = 15%. The optimal weight in the risky portfolio is closest to:
questions.explanation: w^{*} = (0.09 − 0.03)/(4 × 0.0225) = 0.06/0.09 = 66.7%. 133.3% is the weight for A = 2 (halving A by mistake). 40.0% is the Sharpe ratio, not a weight.

questions.stem: R_{f} = 3%. An investor borrows at R_{f} to put 125% of her wealth in a tangency portfolio with E = 9% and σ = 15%. Her portfolio's expected return and standard deviation are closest to:
questions.explanation: E = 3 + 1.25 × (9 − 3) = 10.5%; σ = 1.25 × 15 = 18.75%. 11.25% scales the full 9% by 1.25 and ignores the borrowing cost, while keeping σ unchanged is also wrong. 9.0%/15.0% is the unlevered tangency portfolio.

questions.stem: Three assets have weights 50%, 30% and 20%, standard deviations 20%, 15% and 10%, and pairwise correlations ρ_{12} = 0.5, ρ_{13} = 0.2, ρ_{23} = 0.4. The portfolio standard deviation is closest to:
Which change would make the slope of the capital allocation line steeper?
options: A higher risk-free rate with the tangency portfolio unchanged
A higher expected return on the tangency portfolio with its risk unchanged
questions.explanation: Slope = (E(R_{T}) − R_{f})/σ_{T}. Raising E(R_{T}) increases it. A higher R_{f} lowers the slope, and risk aversion moves the investor along the CAL without changing its slope.

flashcards.back: Part of the minimum-variance frontier above the GMV portfolio: highest return per level of risk.
U = E(R) − ½Aσ^{2}; A > 0 risk averse, A = 0 risk neutral, A < 0 risk seeking.
E(R_{p}) = R_{f} + [(E(R_{T}) − R_{f})/σ_{T}]σ_{p}; slope = Sharpe ratio.

flashcards.front: Optimal weight in the risky portfolio

flashcards.back: The CAL when the risky portfolio is the market portfolio (homogeneous expectations).
Everyone holds the same risky portfolio; risk aversion only decides the mix with the risk-free asset.

modules.title: Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns
modules.summary: Why prices are modelled as lognormal, and how historical simulation, bootstrap resampling and Monte Carlo simulation generate thousands of possible outcomes to value assets and measure risk, including how to set them up in a spreadsheet.

acca.note: Not covered in ACCA beyond simple sensitivity and scenario analysis in PM/FM. Expect conceptual questions on which method to use and one-step calculations with continuously compounded returns.

cards.title: Why lognormal?
cards.body:
If continuously compounded returns are **normal**, the price S_{T} = S_{0} × e^{r} is **lognormal**: right-skewed and never below zero, just like real prices.
